passage:
At five, Kabir crouched over the board game, eyes squeezed shut, whispering to the dice before each throw. "Six, six, six." Lakshmi, his grandmother, watched him blow on them and press his thumbs together. When a six did come up, Kabir shouted that he had made it happen, and when it did not, he tried a longer wish.

At sixteen, at the school fair, Kabir chose his own raffle number, 17, over the one the stall handed him. "Mine is luckier," he told a friend, sure he had tilted the odds by picking it himself.

At twenty, on a betting app at the hostel, Kabir believed his system would beat the chance of the game. When he lost, he put in more to win it back, sure the next round would fall his way. Indu, a hostel mate, watched him for a week and finally sat down. "You've been sure it's about to turn since Monday. Would you talk to someone about it?" Kabir looked at the screen and did not answer at once.

qa.q: What did Kabir whisper to the dice before each throw?
How does Kabir's belief in his own control over chance change from five to twenty?
qa.a: At five Kabir believes wishing and blowing on the dice makes a six; at sixteen he thinks picking his own raffle number tilts the odds; at twenty he believes a system beats the chance of the game and puts in more after each loss. The feeling of being in charge grows into something that keeps him playing.

qa.q: What was Kabir feeling when he put in more money to win back a loss?
qa.a: Kabir felt hopeful and stubbornly confident, sure the next round would fall his way, so he put in more to win the loss back.

qa.q: How could Indu support Kabir after he did not answer at once?
qa.a: Indu could stay calm, keep the talk open without blame, and help Kabir reach a trusted person or a support service if he wants help.

grounding: A child's wishing at dice, a teen's chosen raffle number and a young adult's betting system show the illusion of control over pure chance growing more costly with age.
